(CNN) --     More than 5,000 patients of a South Dakota urology clinic may have been exposed to hepatitis and HIV when the facility reused single-use medical products, state health officials said Friday. Clinic workers told inspectors they've been reusing products since the clinic opened its doors in 2002. The Siouxland Urology Center in Dakota Dunes has been ordered to contact nearly 5,700 former patients treated there since 2002. A routine inspection found the facility was reusing sterile saline bags, tubing and other medical supplies from cystoscopies -- a diagnostic procedure that looks at the lower urinary tract. "We witnessed the practice while we were in the facility," during a January inspection, said Barb Buhler of the South Dakota Health Department. Siouxland Urology has since been put under a provisional license and has been very cooperative, according to state officials. "Siouxland Urology Center informed certain of its patients by U.S. mail that a prior cystoscopy procedure could have potentially exposed them to an infectious disease," the facility's Web site said. It added that "the risk of infection from our past procedure is very minimal and we are unaware of any blood infections in our patients caused by the cystoscopy practice." The clinic, which primarily serves clients from South Dakota, Iowa and Nebraska, is offering free blood tests to those possibly affected to rule out the presence of viruses .Watch more on the possible exposure of urology patients » . On January 21, South Dakota Department of Health inspectors entered an examining room where a cystoscopy was about to take place, and noticed that a saline bag, which was hanging on a pole, was dated January 19, said Bob Stahl, of the South Dakota Department of Health. The inspectors, who are registered nurses, questioned the clinic staff. The clinic staff said they routinely reused saline bags and tubing, although both are clearly marked "for single use only," Stahl said. "They used the bags and tubing on multiple patients," Stahl said. He said the workers at the clinic told the inspectors they'd been reusing bags and tubing since the clinic opened in 2002. They said they didn't see anything wrong with the practice, Stahl said. "It was their standard operating procedure," Stahl said. "They told the inspectors that this was a common practice all over the country. We disagreed and told them this was not a common practice." He said that the clinic had been inspected seven times since it opened, and no one had noticed that the clinic was reusing equipment. "It was just by chance that this saline bag was hanging there. We run across these things by luck at times," Stahl said. "We're fortunate that the team was able to identify this." Fluids from patients can retreat into saline bags and tubing while the equipment is used, and reusing the tubing or saline bags could put patients at risk for contacting diseases from previous patients. A 1-liter bag of saline and tubing costs about $4, according to Mary Jo Lallis, account manager for PSS World Medical, Inc., a medical supply company. CNN's Greg Morrison and Elizabeth Cohen contributed to this report.

# South Dakota Urology Clinic Under Fire for Reusing Single-Use Medical Equipment Since 2002

A South Dakota urology clinic has come under intense scrutiny after health officials discovered that more than 5,000 patients may have been exposed to potentially serious bloodborne pathogens, including hepatitis and HIV, due to a longstanding practice of reusing medical equipment designated strictly for single use.

## Routine Inspection Uncovers Years-Long Practice

The troubling discovery was made during a standard inspection conducted by state health inspectors in January. During their visit, inspectors directly observed clinic staff reusing sterile saline bags and tubing while performing cystoscopy procedures—a practice that had apparently been occurring at the facility since 2002. This routine oversight visit, which might otherwise have gone unremarkable, instead revealed a systemic breach of medical safety protocols that had persisted for well over a decade.

## Facility Response and Regulatory Action

In the wake of these findings, the Siouxland Urology Center has been directed by health officials to reach out to nearly 5,700 former patients who received treatment at the facility since it first opened its doors. As a direct consequence of the violations uncovered during the inspection, the clinic's operating status has been downgraded, and it is now functioning under a provisional license while authorities continue to monitor the situation.

## Staff Acknowledge Violation of Clear Safety Guidelines

Perhaps most concerning is the fact that clinic staff have openly admitted to the practice, acknowledging that they routinely reused saline bags and tubing despite the products being explicitly labeled "for single use only." This admission underscores that the reuse was not the result of confusion or ambiguous labeling, but rather a deliberate departure from manufacturer instructions and standard medical safety practices designed to prevent cross-contamination between patients.

## Clinic's Assurances to Affected Patients

In response to the crisis, the Siouxland Urology Center is now offering free blood testing to all patients who may have been affected by the practice, allowing them to determine whether they have contracted hepatitis, HIV, or other bloodborne infections as a result of their treatment. The facility maintains that the actual risk of infection is minimal, and has emphasized that, to date, there have been no confirmed cases of blood infections directly linked to the reuse of this equipment. Despite these reassurances, the scale of potential exposure—affecting thousands of patients over more than a decade—has raised significant concerns among public health officials and former patients alike regarding oversight and accountability in medical facilities.

# South Dakota Urology Clinic Under Scrutiny After Improper Reuse of Medical Supplies Discovered

A routine inspection conducted in January by health officials uncovered a troubling practice at the Siouxland Urology Center in Sioux Falls, South Dakota: staff members had been reusing single-use medical supplies during cystoscopy procedures, a practice that had apparently been ongoing since the clinic first opened its doors in 2002.

Cystoscopy, a common urological procedure used to examine the bladder and urinary tract, requires the use of sterile equipment to prevent cross-contamination between patients. However, inspectors found that the clinic had been improperly reusing items designated for single-use only, including sterile saline bags and the tubing used to administer them during these procedures. Rather than disposing of this equipment after each patient, as medical protocols require, staff had apparently been using the same supplies across multiple patients over the course of more than a decade.

The implications of this discovery are significant. Health officials estimate that nearly 5,700 patients who underwent cystoscopy procedures at the clinic since 2002 may have been exposed to bloodborne pathogens, including hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV, as a result of this improper reuse of supplies. The reuse of saline bags and tubing creates a pathway for contamination, as bodily fluids or blood from one patient could potentially be transferred to another through the improperly sanitized or reused equipment.

In response to these findings, regulatory authorities took swift action against the facility. The Siouxland Urology Center has been placed under a provisional license, a designation that typically indicates a facility is being closely monitored and must demonstrate corrective actions to address identified deficiencies before regaining full licensing status. This provisional status serves as both a warning and an opportunity for the clinic to overhaul its procedures and ensure compliance with proper medical protocols going forward.

Additionally, in an effort to address the potential health risks to former patients, the clinic has begun offering free blood testing to all individuals who may have been affected by this practice. This testing initiative aims to identify anyone who may have contracted hepatitis or HIV as a result of the contaminated equipment, allowing for early detection and treatment if necessary. Patients who underwent cystoscopy procedures at the facility during the affected time period are being encouraged to take advantage of this free screening to ensure their health and peace of mind.

The case has raised broader questions about oversight and inspection frequency at outpatient medical facilities, as the improper practices went undetected for well over a decade before being discovered during a routine review. Health officials continue to investigate the full scope of the issue and are working to notify all potentially affected patients about the free testing services now available to them.

**SIOUX CITY** — The Siouxland District Health Department has launched an investigation into infection control practices at Siouxland Urology Center after receiving reports that the facility reused single-use saline bags and IV tubing across multiple patients, officials confirmed Tuesday.

The investigation began following a complaint from a former staff member who alleged that saline bags—typically labeled for single-patient use—were being reconnected to new tubing and administered to subsequent patients in an effort to reduce supply costs.

"We take any allegation involving the reuse of single-use medical devices extremely seriously," said **Maria Hensley, Director of the Siouxland District Health Department**. "Saline bags and IV tubing are designed for one patient, one use. When that protocol isn't followed, it opens the door to bloodstream infections and cross-contamination between patients."

According to health officials, inspectors visited the clinic last week to review sterilization logs, supply inventories, and staff interview records. The Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals has also been notified and may conduct a parallel review given the clinic's licensure status.

"Our team is examining whether this was an isolated incident or a systemic practice," said **Dr. Aaron Whitfield, the department's chief epidemiologist**. "We're looking at patient volume over the past 12 months to determine how many individuals may have been exposed and whether any notification or testing is warranted."

In a statement, Siouxland Urology Center said it is "fully cooperating" with investigators and has "temporarily suspended the staff members involved pending the outcome of the review." The clinic did not confirm or deny the specific allegations but stated that "patient safety remains our top priority."

Health officials urged patients who received IV saline treatments at the center within the past year to contact the health department if they experience any signs of infection, including fever, chills, or redness at an injection site.

"We understand this news may be alarming," Hensley said. "Our goal is to be transparent with the public while we determine the facts, and to ensure any necessary corrective action is taken swiftly."

The health department said it expects to release preliminary findings within two to three weeks. No formal citations have been issued at this time.

*This is a developing story. Check back for updates as more information becomes available.*

# State Health Inspectors Find Reused Sterile Supplies at Outpatient Clinic, Prompting Patient Notifications

**RIVERDALE** — State health officials have ordered a local outpatient surgical clinic to notify thousands of former patients after inspectors discovered evidence that single-use sterile supplies were being reused during procedures, according to a report released Tuesday by the Department of Public Health.

The findings emerged from a routine, unannounced inspection last month at Riverdale Same-Day Surgical Center, a facility that performs an estimated 4,000 outpatient procedures annually, including minor orthopedic surgeries and endoscopic exams.

According to the inspection report, surveyors observed staff repackaging and re-sterilizing items labeled "single use only," including certain surgical trays and instrument components not designed to withstand reprocessing. Inspectors also found inconsistent documentation of sterilization cycles and gaps in infection-control logs dating back at least eight months.

"These are precisely the kinds of practices our inspection process is designed to catch," said Dr. Elena Marsh, director of the state's Health Facilities Division. "Reuse of single-use devices can compromise sterility in ways that aren't always visible, creating a real risk of infection transmission."

## Scope of Potential Exposure

Health officials said they are working with the clinic to identify and contact patients who underwent procedures during the period in question. Letters are expected to go out this week advising affected patients to consider bloodborne pathogen testing, including for hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV, out of an abundance of caution.

State officials emphasized that the risk to any individual patient is likely low, but said transparency requires notifying everyone who could have been affected given the scope of the recordkeeping lapses.

"We understand this news is alarming," Marsh said. "But early notification and testing are the best tools we have to identify any issues quickly and get people the care they need."

The clinic has not been formally accused of intentional wrongdoing, and no confirmed cases of infection linked to the facility have been reported as of Tuesday.

## Clinic Response

In a statement, Riverdale Same-Day Surgical Center said it "takes this matter with the utmost seriousness" and is cooperating fully with state regulators.

"Upon learning of the inspection findings, we immediately suspended the reprocessing practices in question and initiated an internal review," the statement read. "Patient safety is our highest priority, and we are committed to full transparency as we work through this process with health officials."

The clinic's medical director, who was not named in the statement, said additional staff training on sterilization protocols has already begun, and an outside infection-control consultant has been retained to audit procedures facility-wide.

The facility remains open, though state officials said several procedure rooms were temporarily closed for review and equipment replacement.

## Regulatory Fallout

The Department of Public Health said it will continue monitoring the clinic through follow-up inspections and has the authority to suspend or revoke its operating license if further violations are found. A corrective action plan is expected to be filed with the state within 10 business days.

Patient advocacy groups said the case underscores the importance of routine, unannounced inspections at outpatient facilities, which have expanded rapidly in recent years as more procedures move outside hospital settings.

"Same-day clinics have become a huge part of how care is delivered," said Renata Ortiz, a patient safety advocate not affiliated with the case. "That makes oversight even more critical, because these facilities don't always have the same layered safety systems a hospital has."

State officials urged any former patients with questions to contact the clinic's dedicated hotline, established this week, or the state health department's consumer protection line.

*This story may be updated as more information becomes available.*
